summary: A tool for analyzing trends in specific regions of the Earth using NASA satellite data. Users select points on an interactive 3D globe, generate a 3D map of the chosen area, and overlay filter layers from the platform’s integrated instruments: MODIS (Terra and Aqua), OMI (Aura, for ozone, NO₂ and SO₂), AIRS (Aqua, for atmospheric temperature, water vapor, CO₂ and CH₄) and GPM (precipitation). Global models add further variables, including MERRA-2 atmospheric reanalysis and GLDAS data on soil moisture, evapotranspiration and runoff. Data is accessed through NASA Earthdata and GES DISC, visualized with NASA Giovanni, and can be complemented with external hydrological datasets such as those from CUAHSI. Built-in temporal and contrast analysis tools help users review and interpret the results. Our goal is to make satellite data accessible to anyone interested in exploring it.
details: Geo-wave is a web tool that turns NASA satellite and model data into clear, verifiable answers about change on Earth. The user starts on an interactive 3D globe, picks a place and a time period (or one of three ready-made events: the 2025 Los Angeles wildfire, the 2025 Kamchatka Mw 8.8 earthquake and the 2024 Málaga flood) and lands on a 3D terrain model with satellite imagery draped over it. There they can switch between 13 data layers (true-color imagery, GPM precipitation, MODIS NDVI, soil moisture, CO, CO₂, NO₂ and ozone), play a timeline across the pre-event, event and post-event phases, compare two dates with a draggable before/after split view, and click any point to see its coordinates, elevation, trend and the physics behind the signal, while color-coded change maps show where change is reliable (orange for a decrease, green for an increase, grey where the data cannot support a conclusion). Its main benefits are that it quantifies change with real units (dB, cm, mm, magnitude), shows a “Sustained real change” badge only when several independent variables agree, keeps real observations apart from interpolated frames, and offers three demo cases that work with no setup. Its intended impact is to make satellite data usable for students, families, journalists and local decision-makers, showing how radar missions like NISAR can see through clouds, smoke and darkness to detect fires, earthquakes and floods, and teaching people to check whether a change is real before trusting it. We built the frontend in JavaScript with React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL for the globe and Three.js with React Three Fiber and custom shaders for the terrain, plus a Python pipeline (NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, Matplotlib, Rasterio) with speckle filtering and confidence masks and a lightweight live API that analyzes any area chosen on the globe, using data from NASA GIBS (MODIS/VIIRS), NASA POWER, MERRA-2, GPM, AIRS, OMI, USGS, NIFC fire perimeters and a terrain elevation model, deployed on Netlify and running in any modern browser with no special hardware. Geo-wave is creative because, instead of flat maps, the user flies from a globe into an animated 3D landscape where the ground actually deforms, burns or floods over time, guided by a story mode and a four-step workflow (Choose event, Explore, Compare, Result), with a plain view for general audiences and a scientific view for experts. The team weighed scientific honesty (all source data is real, but because NISAR is still new, the per-pixel L-band radar signal is a physically based simulation built from real observations and is clearly labelled as such), accessibility (readable text, good contrast, keyboard control and information that never relies on color alone), performance (datasets under 4 MB and the 3D mesh recalculated only when something changes) and ease of use, so the app works even without the live API.
